source.title_on_document: Voice-based debate with an AI adversary is associated with increased divergent ideation

supplement.where: Supporting Information, PDF pp. 10-16; referred to as the SI Appendix in the main text.
supplement.holds: Sample preprocessing and exclusions, conversation counts by modality and AI voice gender, modality-switching analysis, measure construction, statistical methods, and representative transcripts. Main regression coefficients and clustered SEs are in Table 1 on p. 9. The appendix also prints an alternative lexical-diversity coefficient on p. 11. Neither the main text nor this appendix gives numerical outcome estimates for the randomized voice-gender comparison.

paper_design_summary: MBA and EMBA students debated course case questions with CAiSEY, choosing voice or text for each conversation; the analyzed panel contains 203 students and 957 conversations (pp. 2-3, Approach; p. 10, Supporting Information). Fixed-effects regressions compare originality relative to the case reading, verbosity, lexical repetition, and conceptual breadth within user-only conversation text (pp. 9-12). AI voice gender was randomized within voice interactions, but its outcome results are reported only as a general statement of no evidence of an effect (pp. 3, 5, 10).

studies.label: CAiSEY course-debate panel, including embedded randomized AI voice gender

assignment.what_was_assigned: The primary voice-versus-text comparison was self-selected separately for each case discussion. This no code applies to modality. Within selected voice sessions, perceived AI voice gender (female versus male) was randomly assigned (p. 3, Approach; p. 10, Supporting Information). The latter is a nested randomized AI-configuration contrast, not random assignment to voice versus text; details of within-person voice-gender sequences are not provided.
assignment.quote: Because users self-selected their communication modality rather than being experimentally assigned, we cannot make strict causal claims regarding the effect of interface choice on discourse structure.
assignment.locator: p. 3, Approach, second paragraph; p. 10, Supporting Information, Modality Switching Across Successive CAiSEY Sessions

arms.name: Voice-based CAiSEY (self-selected modality)
arms.description: Self-selected spoken debate with CAiSEY; 458 analyzed conversations. This count is outputs, not distinct people. The two voice-gender subconditions below are nested in this arm (p. 10, Supporting Information, Descriptive Statistics).

arms.name: Text-based CAiSEY (self-selected modality)
arms.description: Self-selected typed debate with CAiSEY; 499 analyzed conversations, not distinct people. Reference modality in Table 1; same case materials, prompts, and opposition strategy (p. 3, Approach; p. 9, Table 1 notes; p. 10, Supporting Information).

arms.name: Female AI voice (nested within voice-based CAiSEY)
arms.description: Randomly assigned perceived female AI voice within the spoken modality; 240 conversations assigned. Not an additional independent participant group; distinct people assigned/analyzed in this subcondition are not reported (p. 3, Approach; p. 10, Supporting Information).

arms.name: Male AI voice (nested within voice-based CAiSEY)
arms.description: Randomly assigned perceived male AI voice within the spoken modality; 218 conversations assigned. Not an additional independent participant group; distinct people assigned/analyzed in this subcondition are not reported (p. 3, Approach; p. 10, Supporting Information).

participants.exclusions: The initial dataset included 224 students, not a reported randomized cohort. Excluded 17 who did not use CAiSEY in either study modality and an additional 4 without sufficient data to compute residualized lexical and semantic diversity; the final analyzed sample was 203 students (p. 10, Supporting Information, Sample Preprocessing). No participant-flow counts are supplied separately for the voice-gender outcome analysis.
participants.who: MBA and EMBA students in an elective Technology Strategy course at a top U.S. business school (p. 2, Approach); the acknowledgments identify the participating students as from Columbia Business School (p. 6). Of the analyzed users, 186 of 203 used both modalities (p. 3, Approach). Exact distinct-person counts in each modality or voice-gender subcondition are not stated.
participants.quote: The analytic sample consists of 957 independent CAiSEY conversations generated by 203 MBA and EMBA students across 16 case-based assignments.
participants.locator: p. 10, Supporting Information, Sample Preprocessing and Descriptive Statistics; p. 3, Approach, for modality overlap

ai_tool.name_model: CAiSEY (Classroom Artificial Intelligence Studio for Engaging You); underlying generative model and version not stated (pp. 2-3, Approach).
ai_tool.how_used: An in-house AI debate adversary. After the student selected a stance on a case question, CAiSEY adopted the opposing stance and generated substantive real-time counterarguments in an extended exchange. Students chose voice or text; perceived voice gender was randomized within the voice option. AI remained available throughout production of the scored conversation (pp. 2-3, Approach; pp. 12-16, representative transcripts).

task.description: Generate and defend strategic proposals and arguments in open-ended debates on course case readings. For example, discuss what Netflix should prioritize in its content strategy. Students read a case, choose a position, supply an opening argument, and respond to an AI opponent; the paper explicitly describes the absence of a single right answer. Novelty relative to case materials and conceptual breadth are computed on the student contributions (pp. 2-3, Approach; pp. 11-12, Supporting Information).
task.duration: Across a course term with 16 case-based assignments; per-conversation duration or time limit not stated (p. 2, Approach; p. 10, Supporting Information).

outcomes.name: Divergent ideation: word-count-adjusted semantic diversity
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Conceptual breadth within a single user conversation, not diversity across people. User-only text is divided into 50-word chunks with a 25-word step; all-MiniLM-L6-v2 encodes chunks into 384-dimensional vectors. Upper-triangle cosine similarities between chunks are clipped to [0, 1], normalized, and summarized by Shannon entropy. The primary measure is residualized on word count with user and case fixed effects. Raw semantic diversity is retained as a robustness variant of this outcome, not a separate outcome. These are within-conversation chunk comparisons, so the construct is coded flexibility and diversity_detail is left empty (pp. 11-12, Supporting Information, Divergent Ideation). The observation is one conversation, using only concatenated user messages. OLS includes user and case fixed effects; robust standard errors are clustered by user and case (p. 6, Materials and Methods; p. 9, Table 1 notes; pp. 11-12, Supporting Information).

contrasts.reported: Primary word-count-adjusted semantic diversity, Model 10: coefficient 0.178*** (SE 0.032), p < 0.001. Raw semantic diversity, Model 9: coefficient 1.4*** (SE 0.058), p < 0.001. These are conversation-level regressions: voice N = 458 conversations and text N = 499 conversations, not people.
contrasts.locator: p. 9, Table 1, Models 9-10 and significance legend; p. 4, Findings; p. 12, Supporting Information, Divergent Ideation; p. 10, Supporting Information, Descriptive Statistics of the Study Sample (conversation counts)

outcomes.name: Repetition: word-count-adjusted lexical diversity
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Shannon entropy of the word-frequency distribution within one user conversation. The paper identifies the word-count-residualized measure as primary; residualization uses user and case fixed effects. Unadjusted entropy and the appendix specification that directly controls word count are variants of the same outcome. The adjusted contrast is negative whereas the unadjusted contrast is positive, hence direction is mixed. This is within-output lexical repetition, not diversity across participants or a count of semantic categories. The appendix calls its alternative specification substantively identical, but its printed coefficient differs from Table 1; both are preserved (p. 11, Supporting Information, Repetition). The observation is one conversation, using only concatenated user messages. OLS includes user and case fixed effects; robust standard errors are clustered by user and case (p. 6, Materials and Methods; p. 9, Table 1 notes; pp. 11-12, Supporting Information).

contrasts.reported: Primary word-count-adjusted lexical diversity, Model 8: coefficient -0.042* (SE 0.018), p < 0.05. Raw lexical diversity, Model 7: coefficient 0.262*** (SE 0.023), p < 0.001. Appendix alternative word-count-control specification: beta = -0.105, p < 0.001; no SE printed there. These are conversation-level regressions: voice N = 458 conversations and text N = 499 conversations, not people.

outcomes.name: Repetition: type-token ratio
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Unique words excluding stopwords divided by total words including stopwords, within the concatenated user contribution to one conversation. Lower values indicate greater lexical repetition; the score is neither across-person diversity nor idea fluency (p. 11, Supporting Information, Repetition). The reported sign is retained; no effect size or sign reversal is calculated. The observation is one conversation, using only concatenated user messages. OLS includes user and case fixed effects; robust standard errors are clustered by user and case (p. 6, Materials and Methods; p. 9, Table 1 notes; pp. 11-12, Supporting Information).

eligibility.reason: The principal modality contrast is observational: students chose voice versus text, so it fails random-assignment eligibility (p. 3, Approach; p. 6, Discussion). The overall analyzed dataset has 203 people after exclusions, exceeding the threshold (p. 10, Sample Preprocessing), and originality and within-conversation ideational breadth are computed on their produced arguments (pp. 11-12, measure construction). However, this paper also explicitly randomizes perceived AI voice gender, which may qualify as a nested ai_design experiment; the study gives only conversation assignment counts and a qualitative claim about its outcomes (pp. 3, 5, 10). It does not specify the distinct people analyzed for that contrast or describe their randomized within-person condition sequence. The statement that 186 users used both modalities confirms extensive voice participation, but is not a separately reported participant count for the gender outcome analysis (p. 3). Criterion 1 and paper-level core eligibility are therefore left unclear for adjudication of that embedded comparison; the main voice-versus-text results remain observational regardless. Criterion 2 is met for the reported overall dataset, not a claim that a separate gender-analysis count was supplied. No across-person diversity or post-AI outcome is measured.

one_line_finding: Among 203 analyzed students, self-selected voice debate was associated with greater word-count-adjusted ideational breadth than text debate (coefficient 0.178, SE 0.032, p < 0.001; p. 10, sample counts; p. 9, Table 1, Model 10).
open_questions: Adjudicate the embedded randomized voice-gender comparison as a potential core ai_design experiment: confirm its distinct analyzed participant sample and the assignment/order procedure across repeated voice sessions, and obtain outcome-specific statistics; the PDF supplies only conversation counts and a qualitative null statement (pp. 3, 5, 10).

Resolve the appendix lexical-diversity specification: p. 11 calls the word-count-control result substantively identical but prints beta = -0.105, p < 0.001, whereas the residualized result in p. 9, Table 1, Model 8 is -0.042 (SE 0.018), p < 0.05. Both printed results have been retained as variants.
The generative model/version and data/code repository URLs are not supplied. Page 6 says anonymized data and replication code are available; p. 12 supplies only a live CAiSEY demonstration URL.
notes: One dataset is recorded; the embedded voice-gender subconditions are not counted as a second independent sample. The study design_class and assignment.randomized describe the primary self-selected modality contrast, with the nested randomization explicitly recorded in assignment text, arms, secondary contrasts, and eligibility. The within structure denotes repeated student observations; it does not imply randomized modality order. Table 1 has ten model columns but eight distinct outcomes because raw/residualized lexical and semantic diversity are each grouped. All eight output outcomes are listed. Female versus male is an administrative ordering of the secondary contrast only; the paper identifies neither voice as the proposed/default treatment. Secondary contrast null directions come solely from the general statement on p. 5, not outcome-specific tests. Every n_units value is the overall conversation count from p. 10; gender comparisons concern the voice subset, whose conversation counts are in the nested-arm descriptions. The main Table 1 note calls its modality Ns users, but p. 8, Figure 1 caption and p. 10, sample description establish that these are conversations. No number of people is inferred from an output count. All scored texts contain only user messages (p. 11), and semantic breadth compares chunks within that text, not different people. Figure 1 uses conversation-level Welch tests; the recorded coefficients and SEs instead come from Table 1, whose SEs are clustered by user and case (pp. 8-9). No effect sizes were computed. Data/code fields remain empty because no repository URL is printed (p. 6); the demonstration at https://caisey.me/demo is not coded as a data/code repository (p. 12). The entire markdown, including supporting information and transcripts, was read, and source pages for design, counts, measures, cited results, and disclosures were checked using PDF text extraction.
